articles.title_orig: Live updates: Iran’s president says ‘we will never bow our head’ to Trump in defiant UN speech
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Iran’s president says ‘we will never bow our head’ to Trump in defiant UN speech
articles.content_orig:
• Iran president speaks: In his UNGA address, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will not bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• No breakthrough: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that US-Iran mediated talks on the sidelines of UNGA did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the memorandum of understanding from earlier this year was no longer in the cards.
• Zelensky delivers remarks: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” saying the Russian leader spreads war and instability. As he spoke, Zelensky’s party headquarters were struck by Russia, according to Kyiv officials.
• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on Venezuela to enact reforms.
A recap of Zelensky's key lines in his UNGA speech
During his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin “patient zero,” painting him as the core reason for the war waged against his country.
“Can you even imagine him without war? He is patient zero, the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. And wherever it spreads, it brings only pain, instability, new risks, and of course, new crises,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian leader emphasized that the war is not one that his country chose and called for the end of the conflict and the security of the nation.
Here’s what else Zelensky said during his address:
- The Ukrainian leader said Putin must be denied the space to act and “spread this evil further.”
- He said it was important to target Russia’s financial ability to carry out the war, noting that its oil production is “running out of fumes.” Zelensky added, “Russia’s finances and Russia’s production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped.”
- Earlier in his speech, Zelensky approvingly quoted from a social media post by US President Donald Trump about Russia’s diesel woes.
- Zelensky said Putin’s goal is not just to seize Ukraine’s Donetsk region, he wants more of the country’s cities too.
- Zelensky shared some details of the alleged capture of two North Korean soldiers fighting for Russia who were sent to South Korea. “One of them, when he realized he was he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. He was shocked that fate didn’t let him die,” he said.
CNN’s Max Saltman and Billy Stockwell contributed to this report.
Zelensky touts new drone deals, anti-ballistic program aimed at protecting Europe
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky highlighted on Wednesday Ukraine’s growing partnerships with countries around the world, including a new drone deal signed with Finland.
Zelensky previously said a new drone agreement was ready to be signed in New York, but did not specify which nations were involved.
The Ukrainian leader said that Ukraine, alongside at least nine other nations, have launched a new anti-ballistic program. “Last week, I invited Poland to join, and we are also in consultations with a couple of other allied governments who want to join,” he said.
He said this was part of an effort to build a system that can “become an integrated part of Ukraine’s defense and Europe’s defense” in the future.
Zelensky's party headquarters in Kyiv was struck as he spoke at UNGA
A convention center that hosts the party headquarters of Volodymyr Zelensky was hit in a Russian attack as the Ukrainian leader addressed the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, according to Kyiv city officials.
The strike was the latest in a string of attacks on the country that took place throughout the day.
Attacks in Kyiv killed two people and injured 43 others, city officials said. Among the strikes was one near a university and two on the convention center — the second of which took place as Zelensky spoke.
The roof of the convention center was damaged and the fire resulting from the attack was put out, emergency services said.
Russian forces also dropped four aerial bombs on the Ukrainian village of Oleksandrivka in the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine on Wednesday morning, killing at least five people, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin.
At least six people were reported injured in the bombing, and seven others, including two children, are believed to be trapped under rubble following the morning attack, Filashkin posted to Telegram.
At least 12 apartment buildings, 42 private homes, an administrative building, a kindergarten, a shop and seven vehicles were damaged, he said, adding that search and rescue efforts are ongoing.
Gaza’s reconstruction will take $71.4 billion over next decade, Board of Peace says
The reconstruction of Gaza after years of war will require $71.4 billion over the next decade, the Trump-led Board of Peace said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday.
That estimate dwarfs the $4 to $6 billion the UN said would be required to rebuild Gaza after the 50-day war in 2014.
In a “high-level” briefing in which US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke, members of the board laid out what they pitched as a plan for the first six months of the recovery of Gaza. The plan involves 66 programs, including humanitarian shelters, diesel generators, and rebuilding hospitals. But the board acknowledged the challenges facing the program in that it can only begin “the moment funding and access allow.”
It’s unclear where the funding for the programs will come from, and the technocratic committee intended to administer Gaza — officially called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza — has yet to enter the coastal enclave, instead operating from Cairo, Egypt, with virtually no authority over the territory they are supposed to help govern.
In a statement following the briefing, the Board of Peace boasted that its plan would be led by Palestinians.
But 11 months after President Donald Trump unveiled his 20-point ceasefire plan for Gaza, the effort remains stalled.
Zelensky says Ukraine sent captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea
Ukraine recently sent two North Korean soldiers captured fighting for Russia to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the UN General Assembly.
Zelensky shared some details of the alleged capture, saying “One of them, when he realized he was he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. He was shocked that fate didn’t let him die. This is how they raise people in the north.”
North Korea has sent troops to fight in Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, appearing on the front lines during the Ukrainian invasion of Kursk, Russia. Ukrainian officials recently claimed that North Korea’s troops in Russia include a drone unit to attack targets within Ukraine.
CNN reached out to South Korea and North Korea’s respective UN missions in New York for comment.
Ukraine and Iran are involved in separate but overlapping conflicts
The leaders of Ukraine and Iran spoke at the United Nations General Assembly today amid a pair of ongoing conflicts that, while separate, have contributed to tensions between the countries.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, while Iran has been at war with the US and Israel since late February this year.
Though Tehran and Kyiv are nearly 1,500 miles apart as the crow flies, the wars have overlapping factors, as Iran and Russia are close strategic and military allies.
Many of Russia’s attacks on Ukraine have been carried out using Iranian-made Shahed drones, and Tehran has sent missiles and other weaponry to aid Moscow’s war effort.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, Nasdaq Slip; 10-Year Treasury Hits 19-Year High — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Treasury rates spiked on Wednesday to multiyear highs in what was the biggest one-day move for the 10-year Treasury yield in nearly 18 months. There were a number of reasons cited for the sudden move higher:
- Much stronger-than-expected surveys on U.S. economic activity, especially in the manufacturing sector
- Hawkish commentary from a top Federal Reserve official
- A U.S. Treasury auction for five-year notes that was met with poor demand
- Stubbornly high oil prices with WTI crude rising 2%
The 10-year Treasury note yield popped more than 14 basis points to 5.116% and reached a level not seen since July 2007. The move gained steam after the 10-year yield broke through the key 5% level. It marked the benchmark yield's biggest one-day move since April 7, 2025 — when it surged 16.6 points.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, which is most sensitive to expected changes in Fed policy, jumped more than 12 basis points to 4.906% and hit its highest level since May 2024 as traders increased their bet the Federal Reserve would need to hike again in October.
The 30-year Treasury yield gained more than 10 basis points to 5.41%, the highest levels since mid-2007. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
"This is the market telling us we've entered a genuine re-tightening cycle, said Tony Miano, global investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. "The Fed's 25 basis point hike last week to 3.75%–4% was its first increase since 2023, and the dot plot signaled another this year."
"A week ago you could argue that was a one-and-done insurance move or a one and maybe December hike). Today's price action says investors no longer believe that," he added. Bottom line, "you can't fool or hide in the bond market – unless the Fed gets inflation under control the long end of the curve is going to continue to come under pressure."
Purchasing managers' indexes are typically not huge market movers, but Wednesday morning's readings from S&P Global caught the market off guard. The firm's services PMI jumped to 58.7 in September, its highest level in nearly five years, from 56.5 in August. Its manufacturing counterpart raced to 56.7, a level not seen in more than four years. PMIs are surveys of managers in different sectors across the economy.
"US business continues to boom," S&P Global Market Intelligence chief business economist Chris Williamson said in a statement. "To put the growth surge in context, barring the spike in demand following the opening up of the economy after the COVID-19 lockdowns, the latest improvement in business activity is the greatest recorded since early 2015. Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services."
"Input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices," he added.
Barr's warning, poor auction
Comments from Fed Governor Michael Barr then added even more upward pressure to yields.
"In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion," said Barr. "We want to support sustainable, durable growth in support of maximum employment, and price stability is crucial to that."
Following the first Fed rate hike in more than years last week, odds of another quarter-point rate increase in October rose Wednesday to 70% from 55% a day before, per the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Those chances stood at less than 10% a month ago.
Traders also contended with a much weaker-than-expected Treasury Department auction of 5-year notes. According to BMO, the sale concluded with a yield of 5.033% — far above a six-auction average of 4.186%. Indirect bidders, which include global central banks, scooped up 54% of the auction, well below a 65% average.
"Bottom line, a poor auction with Treasury trying to sell paper into a weak market and where yields weren't attractive enough to bring in the buyers," Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, wrote in a Wednesday note. "The bond bear market continues on."
At the heart of the move higher in yields are persistently higher oil prices. Brent futures rallied more than 3% to trade back above $100 per barrel, while U.S. crude gained more than 2% to $92.86 per barrel.
Oil prices have been soaring this year as the U.S.-Iran war continues, sparking fears of sticky inflation — which may lead to more Fed rate hikes.

articles.title_orig: Hayden Panettiere's death highlights risk of overdose death after stopping and resuming drug use
articles.title_zh: Hayden Panettiere's death highlights risk of overdose death after stopping and resuming drug use
articles.content_orig:
By EVE BUCKLAND and DIANA COOPER, US SENIOR SHOWBIZ REPORTER
Published: 14:49 EDT, 23 September 2026 | Updated: 15:29 EDT, 23 September 2026
Hayden Panettiere was released from a drug rehabilitation facility just weeks before her death from an overdose, per a new report.
Panettiere died aged 36 on August 16 at a residence in Greenville, South Carolina, with her on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother, Zach, both at the scene when Panettiere was pronounced dead.
After it was confirmed that Panettiere accidentally died from the 'toxic effects' of multiple drugs – including fentanyl – a report from The Greenville County Medical Examiner has shed further light on her final weeks.
Per the report obtained by Page Six , one of the two Hickerson brothers – both names are redacted in the report – Panettiere 'was in a drug rehab facility in Malibu, California , up until a few weeks ago.'
One of the brothers also claimed Panettiere had 'a long history of drug, alcohol and nitrous oxide abuse' and that he 'has had to administer Narcan to the decedent before.'
The same brother told the deputy coroner he ' was unsure whether Hayden had consumed illicit drugs in the last two days because she was very good at hiding them.'
Hayden Panettiere was released from a drug rehabilitation facility just weeks before her death from an overdose, per a new report - pictured 2023
Her on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother, Zach, were both at the scene when Panettiere was pronounced dead - pictured 2018
Narcan is a medicine that quickly reverses an opioid overdose and the report reveals two doses of the medicine were administered to the star by Brian after her overdose.
The Daily Mail has contacted the Hickerson brothers, Panettiere and The Greenville County Medical Examiner for further comment.
This comes as harrowing new details about her death from a drug overdose have been laid bare in the report.
The Greenville County Medical Examiner detailed how pressed pills laced with fentanyl were found on a table near her body.
Per the report, first obtained by TMZ , Panettiere was discovered face down in a sitting position on a sofa bed with her legs crossed. She had turned 'deep purple' as the brothers tried and failed to wake her up.
The report notes a senior deputy coroner responded to an Airbnb in Greenville where the actress was staying with the brothers.
One of the brothers said he saw Panettiere applying make-up at 10.30am on the day of her death.
The brother said he then 'went back to bed and was later awakened by a knock at the door.' Moments later, the brothers discovered an unresponsive Panettiere.
After it was confirmed that Panettiere accidentally died from the 'toxic effects' of multiple drugs – including fentanyl – a report from The Greenville County Medical Examiner says  she 'was in a drug rehab facility in Malibu, California, up until a few weeks ago. Pictured 2022
Per the report, the investigator found 'blue pressed pills that tested positive for fentanyl, along with a straw on a table, and white powder in a sunglasses case inside her suitcase.'
Two doses of Narcan were administered to the star by Brian, who then called 911, according to the report.
Panettiere's father Skip was also interviewed, who told investigators the actress had planned to celebrate her 3 7th birthday on August 21 in Greenville before flying to Ukraine to see her daughter.
A spokesman for the Greenville County Coroner’s Office confirmed to The Daily Mail on Tuesday that Panettiere died from the 'toxic effects' of multiple drugs, including fentanyl.
Just a few grains of powerful opioid fentanyl, which is 50 times stronger than heroin, can cause a fatal overdose.
A spokesman said: 'An autopsy was completed by a Board Certified Forensic Pathologist. At autopsy no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to the death.
Hayden Panettiere's cause of death has been officially confirmed, one month after the star died aged 36. Pictured in 2022 in LA
'The cause of death has been ruled as toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol, and Quetiapine. The manner of death has been ruled accident.
'This case is administratively closed by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office.'
Methocarbamol is a prescription muscle relaxant used to treat short-term muscle pain, while Quetiapine, commonly known by the brand name Seroquel, is an antipsychotic prescription medication used to treat conditions including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder.
Alprazolam, known as Xanax, is used to treat anxiety and panic disorders and 4-ANPP is a chemical used as a main building block to make illegal fentanyl.
Last week, insiders told TMZ authorities believed Panettiere had fatally consumed a single oxycodone pill laced with fentanyl.
Panettiere had a 'long time drug dealer' in Los Angeles who she obtained narcotics from illegally, with oxycodone among them, sources told the outlet.
Authorities said that the day prior to her passing, Panettiere had taken multiple drugs she bought in Los Angeles before flying to South Carolina, where she was found dead the next day.
Panettiere's rep said in a statement earlier this month: 'As reported yesterday by the Greenville County Coroner's Office, Hayden's death remains under investigation pending the completion of toxicology results, despite reports from some outlets stating otherwise.
'Recent reports attributed to unnamed sources are unverified hearsay and have attributed to conflicting information that continues to circulate.'
The statement continued: 'While we are all eager to find closure and better understand the circumstances surrounding her passing, we must remain patient and allow the investigative process to unfold.'
Panettiere is survived by a daughter, Kaya, now 11, who shares with ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko – pictured 2011
In 2018, when her daughter Kaya was three, she signed full custody to her ex amid her battle with postpartum depression and addiction and Wladimir moved their daughter to his native Ukraine
The late Heroes star's rep concluded in saying that 'the answers we are all seeking will come.'
On the day she died, first responders arrived at a Greenville, South Carolina, condo where attempts were made to resuscitate the actress, before she was pronounced dead.
Hickerson's lawyer Sloan Ellis said in a statement August 20 that 'Hayden's death remains under investigation and it is important to allow that investigation to proceed.
'As has been publicly reported, police confirmed there were no signs of foul play. Out of respect for Hayden's loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time.'
Panettiere began acting as a child, appearing in soap operas, then gained wider recognition for her role in the 2000 sports drama Remember the Titans with Denzel Washington, and as the voice of Dot in Pixar's 1998 film A Bug's Life.
Panettiere is remembered for her role as Claire Bennet on the hit NBC series Heroes
She played Juliette Barnes on the ABC show Nashville, releasing a number of her own songs
Panettiere later found fame playing cheerleader Claire Bennet in the superhero drama Heroes before starring as country singer Juliette Barnes for six seasons on Nashville.
She earned two Golden Globe nominations for best supporting actress on the show, while her singing produced 11 entries on the US Billboard Hot Country Songs charts.
Panettiere's film credits include 2006's Bring It On: All or Nothing, the comedy-drama film Raising Helen, and appearances in Scream 4 and Scream VI as Kirby Reed.
She had an 11-year-old daughter called Kaya following a life-threatening birth, and later gave full custody of the child to her former fiancé, Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko.
Panettiere's passing was announced by her father Skip Panettiere, who said in a statement: 'It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden.
'She was an incredible light

articles.title_orig: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
articles.title_zh: ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club
articles.content_orig:
The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.”
The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies.
Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club.
Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”.
The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries.
European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit.
Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended.
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.”
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.”
Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped.
Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”.
Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices.
In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress.
Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy.
“President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet.
For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens.
On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke.
A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station.
Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well.
In response to what has happened, the House foreign affairs committee posted on X: “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.”
Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv

articles.content_orig:
Iran War Updates: U.S. and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump threatens regime with annihilation
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, saying Iranians are "the victims of terrorism" by the U.S. and Israel, and have "never ever been an aggressor."
- A commercial vessel was struck in an attack in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, killing one crew member and necessitating the evacuation of more than 20 more sailors, according to the Omani navy.
- The Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened Wednesday to attack U.S. interests in the Middle East and to "close Bab el-Mandeb completely to American ships" if Washington joins Saudi-led military operations against the group in Yemen.
White House responds to Iranian president's speech at U.N.
President Trump is "courageously" fighting against the Iranian regime, the White House said Tuesday in response to a question about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's speech at the U.N. General Assembly.
"The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," Anna Kelly, White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable."
Through a translator, Pezeshkian said Iran was a victim of Israel and the U.S., and the U.S. is using the Strait of Hormuz "to impose their aggression upon us."
Iran "will never bow our head or bend at the knee. Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialog and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," Pezeshkian said.
Canada imposes new sanctions on Iran officials, entities
The Canadian government announced new sanctions Wednesday against several senior Iranian officials and state-run entities "for their role in the Iranian regime's brutal repression of its population."
The sanctions target five senior Iranian security and government officials and five state-run entities, the foreign ministry said in a statement, without providing specifics.
"These individuals and entities have contributed to Iran's efforts to suppress dissent and restrict fundamental freedoms of Iran's population, including through digital surveillance, censorship, unlawful violence, arbitrary detention and intimidation," the ministry said.
A protest movement in Iran sparked in late December by grievances over high living costs rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on Jan. 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths from the unrest, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.Rights groups based abroad put the toll higher and accused security forces of firing at demonstrators.
Massive protests also erupted in Iran in Sep. 2022 following the death in custody of Iranian Kurdish woman Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested for allegedly violating strict dress rules for women.
UAE sanctions local branches of Iran's Bank Melli
The UAE central bank said Wednesday that it had imposed sanctions on the Emirati branches of Iran's Bank Melli, accusing it of violating local laws on money laundering, terrorism and arms proliferation.
The bank said in a statement that "it has been decided to prohibit all branches of Bank Melli Iran operating in the UAE from conducting any financial transactions to and from Iran, including trade finance and fund transfers."
It cited "non-compliance with the regulations, laws and supervisory decisions in force in the UAE, including the requirements and obligations set out under the legislation related to combating money laundering, the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing."
The announcement comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, as well as Washington's more recent economic pressure campaign against the Islamic Republic.
As part of that stepped-up campaign, the U.S. announced new measures at the end of August targeting Iran's trading partners, and sanctioned the director of the Dubai branch of Bank Melli.
Last month, the United Arab Emirates announced the suspension of trade and financial exchanges with Tehran.
German foreign minister: "Iran must engage constructively" in negotiations
Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, offered a direct criticism of Iranian negotiations in a meeting with his counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on Tuesday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Iran must engage constructively in talks for a sustainable solution to end the conflict in the region & unconditionally open the Strait of Hormuz, ensuring free, safe and toll-free navigation for all," he said on social media.
Wadephul's comments came as Iran continues to take a hard line in negotiations, demanding the U.S. remove its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, end the war on all fronts, release frozen or restricted assets and agree to the Oman-Iran negotiated passage through the strait, according to Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.
Araghchi has yet to comment on the meeting with Wadephul, though the government shared photo of the two meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
Tehran reviewing U.S. response to its proposal, senior Iranian official tells Reuters
Iran is reviewing a U.S. response to its plan to end the fighting between the two countries, a senior Iranian official told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday, adding that many differences remain between the two sides.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the ending of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels were subjects discussed during indirect talks with the U.S. on Tuesday, the official said.
Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei said Wednesday in a long interview aired by state television network IRIB that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the U.S. met Iran's long-stated conditions.
"There is no staging or step-by-step process," he said. "Iran is trying to have this implemented within three or four days, within four or five days, for example."
"The next step will also be determined and specified by the Islamic Republic of Iran," Rezaei said.
Iran has long demanded the U.S. lift its blockade and return to the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June by President Trump and his Iranian counterpart, which Tehran quickly accused the U.S. of breaching by keeping the blockade in place.

The U.S. Department of Justice late Tuesday evening urged a federal judge not to block President Donald Trump's total ban of three news outlets from the White House, saying, "Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."
The DOJ, in a new court filing, also said Trump was motivated by concerns about national security in his decision Friday to summarily ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House.
The filing came ahead of Wednesday's scheduled teleconference hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., where Judge Timothy Kelly will hear arguments by a lawyer for the outlets, which have asked him to enjoin Trump from continuing the ban as part of a lawsuit filed against him Monday.
"The President has determined that Plaintiffs have reported classified or sensitive information bearing on national security," the DOJ said in the filing to Kelly, who is a Trump appointee.
"The President therefore has a compelling interest in limiting access to White House grounds to organizations that do not pose such a risk to national security," the filing says.
Targeting claims by the media outlets in their lawsuit, the DOJ said that there is no First Amendment right of news reporters to the White House.
The outlets in their suit say that Trump's ban was motivated by so-called viewpoint discrimination, or targeting them for their perceived "motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective."
The DOJ, in its filing, included new letters, dated Tuesday, to the media outlets, giving each of them to chance to contest the initial decision to ban them and the factual basis for the ban.
The letters reference stories published by the outlets that purportedly threatened national security.
"Plaintiffs may submit any response by 5:00 pm on Friday, September 25, 2026," the filing says.
"Otherwise, 'this initial decision will be final."

articles.title_orig: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.title_zh: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be lifted immediately.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing.
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
The news organizations are scheduled to make their case to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly at a 3:30 p.m. ET hearing.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.
On Tuesday, the White House Press Office sent letters to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” the department said in the filing. The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
The outlets did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the allegations in the filing.
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend of the court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups that took part in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday, and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool.
CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage, resulting in Trump’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House being inaudible.
His remarks at the United Nations on Tuesday and alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference Monday were picked up by U.N. cameras and local news outlets, respectively.
Trump defended the bans in a social media statement Monday and added a new argument — that “fake news” is a national security issue.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years on New York sex crime conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years in prison Wednesday, more than a year after a jury found the former Hollywood mogul guilty of sexually assaulting former “Project Runway” production assistant Miriam Haley in a high-stakes retrial.
Weinstein appeared in the downtown Manhattan courtroom in a wheelchair, his hands cuffed to his seat.
In a victim impact statement read aloud in the courtroom, Haley said Weinstein “abused his position and power,” causing a “devastating effect on my life and security.”
“It is a life sentence for me,” Haley said.
Weinstein also addressed the court, again denying the allegations against him while apologizing to “anyone I may have hurt by my actions.” He had pleaded not guilty to a charge of first-degree criminal sexual act.
“I am not a perfect person,” he said, “but I am a person who has made mistakes.” He later added: “I am not a violent man.”
Judge Curtis Farber excoriated Weinstein before handing down his sentence. “You took what you wanted by force, and you have never accepted responsibility,” the judge told the former entertainment industry kingmaker.
Farber said Weinstein’s 15-year sentence will be followed by five years of supervised release and a requirement that he register as a sex offender.
Wednesday’s sentencing came after a protracted series of trials, appeals and courtroom proceedings that have kept Weinstein behind bars since his arrest in 2018, one of the key events of the #MeToo movement.
“Today was about the survivors,” Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg said in a statement, adding: “I’m moved, as we should all be moved, by their courage and their steadfastness through what has obviously been a challenging process.”
Weinstein was originally convicted in 2020 of third-degree rape involving former aspiring actor Jessica Mann and first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley. He was sentenced to 23 years in prison. But his conviction was overturned in 2024 by a New York state appeals court, and a judge ordered a new trial.
Weinstein was again found guilty in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act involving Haley, who testified that he forcibly performed oral sex on her in his New York City apartment in 2006. The same jury acquitted him of a separate criminal sex act charge involving allegations from former model Kaja Sokola.
The jurors at Weinstein’s second New York trial could not reach a verdict on the charge related to Mann’s allegation, and a third trial on that charge also ended in a hung jury. In late June, prosecutors declined to try the Mann case a fourth time.
Weinstein was separately convicted in Los Angeles in December 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault related to a 2013 assault of an Italian actor and model. He was sentenced by a Los Angeles judge to 16 years in prison in February 2023.
He is set to be resentenced in L.A. after an appeals court vacated his original sentence.
The former producer and film distributor vehemently denies all allegations of sexual misconduct, insisting his sexual encounters were consensual. In all, more than 80 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault or harassment.
Weinstein once lorded over Hollywood. Miramax, his first distribution label, released seminal independent films like “Clerks” and “Pulp Fiction.” He won an Oscar as a producer of “Shakespeare in Love.” In the early 2010s, his second distribution company scored back-to-back best picture wins for “The King’s Speech” and “The Artist.”
But his reign came crashing down in 2017 after The New York Times and The New Yorker published exposés detailing his alleged pattern of sexual harassment and assault. The first wave of accusations against him in 2017 propelled the #MeToo movement, a reckoning with sexual misconduct by powerful people in high-profile professions.
In recent years, Weinstein’s health has visibly declined, and he has faced various medical issues, including diagnoses of bone marrow cancer, kidney disease and diabetes. He has been held at the Bellevue Hospital prison ward, and he will remain there until he is sent to a state prison.

Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.
The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
"It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media.
The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks.
The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight".
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
The months-in-the-making clash between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Benjamin Netanyahu will come to a head on Thursday when the Israeli prime minister delivers a speech before the U.N. General Assembly in Manhattan.
The two are poised to become the focal point of the annual gathering of the world’s most powerful people, which brings motorcades, gridlock and demonstrations to the city. This year’s event comes with an additional layer of drama: During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani threatened to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant. The mayor later clarified he doesn’t have the authority to arrest the prime minister, but has still called him a “war criminal.”
In a CNN interview released on Tuesday, Mamdani maintained his criticism, saying the warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity is “something that should be honored, because what we want to see, and we’ve been talking about this today, is a faith in our politics, a faith in accountability.”
Netanyahu teased his upcoming remarks on Tuesday with a video where he falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers. He also delivered a direct message to Mamdani. “I'm coming to the U.N.,” he said. “I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm going to tell the truth about you.”
Asked about the video, the mayor called Netanyahu the “architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians” and referenced ongoing Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The NYPD has warned protests are anticipated near the U.N. on Manhattan's East Side throughout the General Assembly. Mamdani has said he won’t attend protests against Netanyahu — noting he would uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Sal Albanese, a former city councilmember who advised Mamdani on public safety, said he believed the mayor could balance the two interests of politics and public safety. Mamdani’s pro-Palestinian activism is a key part of his identity that fueled his election and continued popularity, he said. Similarly, protests are a fixture of the city.
“Netanyahu is obviously going to drive a lot of people on the street to protest,” he said. “As long as they do it peacefully, I don’t think it will be a problem.”
In July, Jewish leaders criticized the mayor for inflaming tensions with his criticism of Israel following the stabbings of a Jewish man and an Asian man on the Upper West Side. The attack occurred days after Mamdani had released a video acknowledging that he did not have the legal authority to order Netanyahu’s arrest. Nevertheless, he said Netanyahu was a “war criminal.”
This is not the first time a New York City mayor has clashed with a foreign leader in town for the General Assembly. In 1995, Mayor Rudy Giuliani directed his Chief of Staff Randy Mastro to ask Yasir Arafat, then the chair of the Palestine Liberation Organization, to leave a Lincoln Center concert. The Clinton administration issued a statement criticizing Giuliani’s actions.

articles.title_zh: Where a powerful nor’easter could hit hardest this weekend
articles.content_orig:
Nor'easter's flooding, strong winds a threat from NC to New England
Coastal flooding is already affecting parts of the mid-Atlantic as the powerful nor'easter crawls up the East Coast.
A nor'easter will bring coastal flooding, high surf, wind and rain to parts of the East Coast through the weekend, with impacts from North Carolina and the Virginia Tidewater, to the Jersey Shore and New England.
The nor'easter hasn't yet gained strength. But the pressure difference between low pressure off the East Coast and high pressure over eastern Canada is driving gusty winds along the Eastern Seaboard.
Some gusts are topping 40 mph along the coast from southern New Jersey and Delaware to the Virginia Tidewater.
And those persistent winds are piling water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday morning's high tide.
Flooding was reported Wednesday morning in downtown Norfolk, Smithfield and Suffolk, Virginia, according to the National Weather Service.

Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days.
- Through Thursday: Coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds from New Jersey to northern Outer Banks of North Carolina
- Friday: Rain, possibly heavy, stronger winds, and coastal flooding arrive in parts of southeast New England, Long Island; coastal flooding at high tide, gusty winds continue from New Jersey to Virginia Tidewater, northern North Carolina.
- Saturday: Locally heavy rain, strong winds possible over much of coastal, southern New England. High tide coastal flooding from New England to at least parts of the mid-Atlantic coast once again. Some at least light bands of rain possible as far west as Hudson Valley, New Jersey.
- Sunday: Nor'easter weakens, but rain showers, some gusty winds could linger over much of New England, possibly the Hudson Valley.
- Monday: Some showers could linger in parts of New England and upstate New York.
The map below shows the severity of coastal flooding forecast at high tide through Friday night or early Saturday, color coded by severity.
The most significant coastal flooding will be from the southern New Jersey shore to the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina, including the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay.
This flooding will happen for multiple high tides, possibly five or more, into at least early this weekend in these areas.
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is possible along stretches of these beaches.
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will also develop in parts of New England by late Friday into the weekend.
We expect the heaviest rain to fall over coastal New England from Friday through the weekend.
This could lead to flash flooding, especially in urban areas, including the Boston metro.
It could also compound any coastal flooding at high tide in parts of southeast New England.
Much lighter rainfall accumulations are expected farther west, in the light green colors in the map below.
In the New York City metro, the heaviest rainfall is expected in eastern Long Island, with less rain farther west in the New Jersey suburbs.
The strongest winds with this nor'easter are expected this weekend from coastal and southeast New England to eastern Long Island, with some gusts over 50 mph possible, at times.
In these areas, some tree damage and power outages are most likely, including the Boston metro, Providence and Cape Cod.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible farther down the coast from the Jersey Shore to Delaware, and the Virginia Tidewater. Some sporadic power outages and tree limb damage are also possible in these areas.
Here are some tips to keep in mind if you plan to travel to the Northeast into this weekend:
- Northeast major hub airports: Delays are most likely at Boston-Logan this weekend and are possible, at times, at NYC's three major airports through the weekend.
- Roads: Some downed trees or tree limbs and flash flooding are possible in southeast and coastal New England, as well as eastern Long Island. Avoid coastal areas from northern North Carolina to southeast New England around any high tides into the weekend.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter?)
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

articles.title_orig: EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires
articles.title_zh: EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires
articles.content_orig:
The EU has agreed to remove two Russian billionaires, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from its sanctions list, while extending restrictions on nearly 3,000 individuals and companies accused of supporting the war on Ukraine for the next three years.
With an end-of-Tuesday deadline looming to preserve the Russia blacklist, the EU’s 27 member states found a compromise that meant delisting the two oligarchs in spite of very few countries wanting this outcome. EU sanctions have to be approved unanimously.
France stunned and infuriated EU governments this month when it called for Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek national, to be removed from the list on “national security” grounds, reported to refer to a prisoner exchange deal involving French nationals and Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg then asked for the same treatment for Fridman, the Russian-Israeli magnate, who is suing the Grand Duchy for $16bn (£12bn) for freezing his assets.
The exemptions angered many EU countries which believe it sets a bad precedent by allowing member states to weaken sanctions in defence of national interests.
Ukraine criticised the removal of the men from the sanctions list as unacceptable. Shortly after the decision emerged, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on social media: “No name on the sanctions list is there by accident: each one represents a reason why this war started and continues to this day.”
The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, called the decision “shameful and unjustifiable” on X. “Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he added.
In order to enable the delistings that many EU member states found unpalatable, it was proposed that the sanctions be rolled over for 36 months, rather than the usual six.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s EU presidency, which brokered the talks, said the bloc had reached “a difficult compromise”. They said: “Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
A decision had been expected earlier this week, but Latvia’s government, facing parliamentary elections on 3 October, announced a last-minute objection to the delistings on Monday. Latvia’s prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, said late on Monday night that he could not accept the proposed compromise and instructed his foreign minister to enter talks with Paris and Brussels to find a solution.
Diplomats said Latvia had finally agreed to abstain on the two delistings. The blacklist includes Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, as well as Duma deputies, the country’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex.
Senior EU officials have promised to present about 1,600 new designations – individuals and entities involved in the Russian military industrial complex – to foreign ministers next month. But the latest standoff, which followed the tortuous agreement on the EU’s 21st round of sanctions in July, suggests the process could be difficult.

The original Blue Yeti has been one of the most recognizable go-to USB microphones for content creators since it launched in 2009, and now it finally has a successor. Launching today under Logitech G, the Blue Yeti 2 adds some modern upgrades, including an interactive LED display, AI de-noising, and a proximity based voice sensor — which resolves a notable flaw with its predecessor’s design while still paying homage to it.
Logitech’s new Blue Yeti 2 mic adjusts itself to where you are
The Blue Yeti’s successor is (hopefully) idiot-proofed for podcasters, YouTubers, and anyone else trying to be heard.
It’s available in black or white color options for $159.99, which is comparatively cheaper than Shure’s popular MV7 series USB microphones, which are the current choice for podcasters and start at $299. It’s also interestingly just $10 more than the original Blue Yeti’s launch price 17 years ago. A lot has happened since then, with Logitech acquiring the Blue audio production company for $117 million in 2018 and later killing the Blue brand entirely in 2023 when it merged the products with its own gaming-focused Logitech G sub brand. That means this new launch should just be called the Yeti 2, but Logitech clearly has some nostalgia to play with here.
The Blue Yeti 2 includes a built-in audio proximity sensor that tracks your voice in 3D, and automatically adjusts gain, EQ, and pickup patterns to preserve recording quality regardless of how close or far you are when moving around the mic. That should make this a more beginner friendly USB microphone than the original, as you don’t need to have any knowledge or experience with manually tweaking those settings to achieve optimal results. Plus, it still retains a similar design to the OG Yeti which confused people into incorrectly speaking into the top of it, an issue this new sensor should address.
It provides up to 24-bit / 48 kHz high-resolution capture. Other audio features include integrated direct digital signal processing (DSP) to improve voice clarity without additional software, and AI-powered noise removal to reduce unwanted background sounds like computer fans and mouse clicks. Given Logitech is pitching this to streamers, the 1.3-inch color LED display on the front where the controls are located also features a “Yeti character” that provides visual feedback on gain levels and polar patterns.

articles.title_orig: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.title_zh: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.content_orig:
When the White House ballroom was hit with a legal challenge in December, Donald Trump’s defense of his pet project shifted from “I need a place to throw lavish parties” to “the White House needs a military complex, complete with an underground medical facility and rooftop drone port, and every day we go without one is a national security risk.”
But it turns out the safety threat is coming from inside the White House.
The Washington Post reports that original ballroom architect James McCrery II resigned last year after Trump kept pushing design features that violated safety codes. And these weren’t minor burdensome regulations, like stipulations on the exact size of the restrooms (though one early design did feature just seven women’s stalls for 650-plus guests). We’re talking about design features meant to keep everyone alive in an emergency:
Trump’s growing vision for the ballroom triggered a cascade of design issues, including conflicts with building standards McCrery was trained to follow, according to the people familiar with their discussions.
McCrery informed the White House that Trump’s ballroom design did not meet fire safety codes, which require the majority of guests to be able to quickly exit through the main entrance during an emergency, according to the people and documents. The architect also pointed out that alternative emergency exit routes out of the building were insufficient, and that there was little in the design to prevent a kitchen fire from rapidly spreading into the event space on the floor above.
The ballroom and other Trump construction projects are being run out of the Executive Residence rather than the federal agencies that would usually handle White House renovations and ensure building-safety standards are being met. Trump reportedly made it clear his own desires came first:
Trump brushed off McCrery’s concerns, they said, and the president countered that no building codes apply to White House construction.
“I am the code,” Trump said.
Trump’s L’État, c’est moi attitude has always been deeply concerning, but this is the first suggestion that it could put hundreds of people’s lives in imminent danger.
It’s unclear why exactly McCrery left the project. It was previously reported that he left due to Trump’s repeated demands to make the ballroom bigger. McCrery released a statement on Tuesday saying he’s “truly grateful” for getting a chance to work on the ballroom. A White House spokesman said in a separate statement that it would be “factually false and totally inaccurate” to say that “McCrery’s departure from the project was in any way associated with code issues.”
McCrery wasn’t the only person pointing out that Trump’s ever-evolving design plans were creating safety problems. (The Post obtained Sharpie-scrawled blueprints, which were stored in a box marked “Docs bearing POTUS’s mark,” showing Trump was deeply involved in the process.) A White House official’s notes from a September 2025 meeting to review ballroom plans say, “Life safety — big concern.” Documents from weeks later suggest administration officials were still working to get Trump’s “buy in” on not having hundreds of White House guests die in a fire:
In the months that followed his resignation, documents show, the White House team continued to discuss life-safety issues and a code review for the ballroom project. It is unclear if a review was ever completed.
“Life safety — needs POTUS buy in,” read one White House official’s notes from a Nov. 6 meeting on the project.
It’s unclear if these “life safety” issues were ever resolved. Shalom Baranes Associates, the new architecture firm working on the project, declined to comment. But the Post notes the contract between the White House and Clark Construction, the firm actually building the ballroom, does say it must comply with local, state, and federal codes, and a third party has been tasked with ensuring that happens:
Clark has hired a private company to do third-party inspection of the construction, according to a memo notifying the White House of its plan to issue a no-bid subcontract for the work.
A spokesperson for Clark Construction, the project’s general contractor, said in a statement, “As demonstrated by our successful history delivering projects for Federal clients across the United States, we consistently follow applicable building codes and life safety requirements.”
So hopefully someone is making sure that the new White House ballroom/military complex isn’t a gilded death trap, even if Trump doesn’t really care.

Gary Cohn, vice chair at tech giant IBM (IBM) and former economic adviser to President Trump, isn't yet ready to use Meta's (META) new Muse AI agent in his daily life.
And surely he isn't alone on this front.
"I'm not comfortable giving up my personal data and my personal information," Cohn said on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed. "By the way, I have enough trouble managing my life, knowing my own personal data. I don't like giving it to someone else, that's not in my comfort zone right now."
Meta investors have been having a week to remember as Muse has surged to the top spot on Apple's App Store.
Muse reached 2.8 million downloads in its first 12 days across both the US and Canada app stores, according to the latest Sensor Tower data.
What's more, Muse has surpassed ChatGPT in early adoption, with 1.8 million downloads in Muse's first 12 days compared to 1.3 million for ChatGPT. Muse also set a new US daily download record of 264,000 on Sept. 19, its third straight day above 200,000.
Shares of Meta have rallied by some 20% over the past two weeks as Muse mania has taken hold across markets and social media.
Now all eyes turn to CEO Mark Zuckerberg at his annual Meta Connect event later today. Investors have high expectations for how Muse will be integrated into Meta's smart glasses, and they also hope to get fresh download and usage data.
"The most important update from Zuck's Meta Connect keynote that kicks off tonight at 7pm ET has nothing to do with wearables," longtime tech analyst Gene Munster wrote in an X post. "Investors will be eagerly waiting for him to share any datapoints on Muse's early adoption. For all the buzz that Muse has gotten, pushing shares of up 20% over the past two weeks, the company has shared little."
Munster added, "Alexandr Wang, Meta's Chief AI Officer, has said usage is running 'well ahead of internal projections' and he framed it as the biggest consumer AI launch since ChatGPT, with heavier U.S. download volume than Threads, WhatsApp, and Facebook combined. So tonight will be the first time we hear from Zuckerberg on Muse. Fingers crossed for some juicy data points."

New Marvin Harrison Jr. Trade Rumors on Cardinals WR Amid Struggles to Start 2026 NFL Season
Teams around the NFL are keeping an eye on wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr.'s status with the Arizona Cardinals, according to ESPN's Dan Graziano.
Graziano reported Wednesday that "execs around the league are wondering whether the Arizona Cardinals could explore trading" Harrison.
"Harrison is extension-eligible after this season, and as of now, the Cardinals would have a hard time paying him based on what he's shown in the league so far," Graziano reported. "It's worth watching out for a potential change-of-scenery deal in this case."

Contracts That Teams Already Regret 💸
Harrison, the No. 4 pick of the 2024 draft, is currently signed through the 2027 season with a 2028 club option on his rookie contract. He has made one catch for 33 yards through two games of his third NFL season.
Harrison was targeted twice in Week 2, although one target was erased due to a penalty and he made no receptions in the Cardinals' 31-7 loss to the visiting Seattle Seahawks.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said after Sundays's loss he didn't see Harrison's lack of production as connected to any issues with his effort level.
"The spots he was trying to get to, he was getting to, we just weren't able to connect," LaFleur said.
LaFleur continued, "I know it's like, 'Well, just get some easy completions to get going.' And that's fine. You also have Trey McBride, who's one of the best underneath guys in the world, and there's only about 60, 65 plays a game."
He added it was a "long season" and indicated he felt Harrison could see more usage in the future depending on the defensive scheme of the teams the Cardinals line up again.
McBride has gotten the largest target share among Jacoby Brissett's pass-catchers so far this season, hauling down 17 receptions on 23 targets for 136 yards and two touchdowns.
Among Cardinals receivers, most targets have gone to veteran wideout Kendrick Bourne and Michael Wilson Jr., the latter of which signed a three-year, $75 million extension with $47 million guaranteed earlier this month.
McBride signed his own extension last offseason, giving the Cardinals two long-term pass-catching options even if the franchise decides to move on from Harrison.
The Cardinals could potentially receive increase trade interest in Harrison should he see more usage ahead of the deadline. Whether the franchise will actually consider selling in November could depend on how LaFleur is able to help his team build on their 1-1 start, starting Sunday with a road game against the 2-0 San Francisco 49ers.

articles.title_orig: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Garoppolo and 4 other names for NFL teams in need of a quarterback - The Athletic
