China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
ICIJ’s media partners uncovered strategic deals and moves the Chinese bank made around the world to further the political priorities of the party-state.
China Capital, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in collaboration with 23 media partners, provided an unprecedented look into decision-making at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, one of the most powerful Chinese institutions, at a time of China’s ascendance on the world stage.
The investigation is based on more than 4.8 million confidential records from two of ICBC’s U.K. units. The records provide rare insight into one of China’s most important financial arms, showing how the government’s influence and political priorities often outweigh ordinary banking protocols.
This is the first time that an international team of reporters has examined the inner workings and lending practices of ICBC– the world’s largest bank by asset size. Like many of its state-owned peers, ICBC is notoriously secretive.
“The ICIJ investigation shows how branch structures can be leveraged by foreign bank headquarters to override local compliance officers when state-backed corporate interests conflict with local regulatory obligations,” said David P. Weber, an accounting professor at West Virginia University and former Chief Investigator of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He urged regulators in the U.S. and the U.K. to implement a cross-border enforcement mechanism that could “reduce oversight fragmentation.”
From New Zealand to Mexico, the 75 journalists who participated in the investigation uncovered previously unknown details about the bank’s involvement in some of their countries’ most important infrastructure projects and natural resources companies, as well as deals with firms linked to China’s military apparatus. Here are some of the revelations they uncovered.
The bank did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
How ICBC blended commercial interests with China’s political priorities
ICIJ’s partners across India, New Zealand and Austria found repeated instances where the bank’s political role blended with its commercial interests.
In 2017, Indian and Chinese troops reached a stand-off in the disputed Doklam region at the two countries’ borders, after the Indian government accused Beijing-backed companies of building roads in a territory claimed by China and Bhutan, in violation of a 1980 treaty. The two-month face-off didn’t just have political repercussions, The Indian Express, an ICIJ partner, reported. It also triggered actions inside ICBC’s Mumbai branch, more than 1,200 miles south of the border.
Soon after the news reached the bankers, ICBC “suspended the disbursement of 11 approved but undisbursed loans and bond investments totalling $185 million,” according to internal records. The bank also “organized” Chinese Communist Party members across every department to stay in constant touch with China’s embassy and consulate. The incident exemplifies the bank’s tight links to the party-state and how geopolitical events can influence its lending operations around the world.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations advance the party’s interests, and some bankers were internally referred to as “comrades.”
In New Zealand, The Post reported that a Communist Party member who worked as a senior executive at ICBC’s Auckland outpost handled the local accounts of Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance tech company with links to the government. Numerous investigations by researchers and journalists have documented how, since at least 2017, Hikvision has provided surveillance technology to forces in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where Xi Jinping’s government has waged a repression campaign against hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. In 2020, the U.S. government blacklisted the firm for enabling human rights abuses.
Internal ICBC records describe how Lu Ping, the chief marketing officer of the ICBC subsidiary in New Zealand, “exhibited the outstanding qualities of a communist party member.” “Comrade Lu Ping” was nominated for a company-wide commendation in 2022 for his proactive role “fulfilling cash management needs” in New Zealand for Hikvision and Huawei, one of the bank’s most important clients.
China Capital also uncovered secret links between one of Austria’s most important aviation companies and a top Chinese producer of military aircraft. ICIJ’s partner in Vienna, profil, examined internal 2021 memos that discussed a $230 million loan to Future Advance Composite Components, which is affiliated with the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China.
While FACC, as the firm is known, publicly states that it produces aircraft parts exclusively for the civilian market, its Chinese owner has an “absolute leading position” in China’s defense industry and is the “sole manufacturer of all kinds of military aircraft and airborne equipment” in the country, according to the records.
ICBC bankers also discussed the possibility that the U.S. government could sanction AVIC in the future due to its links to China’s military apparatus. Though some London officers opposed extending the loans due to risk management concerns, they left the ultimate decision to ICBC’s Beijing headquarters. The documents do not state whether the bank approved the loan. AVIC did not respond to inquiries from profil.
Strategic deals revealed across Australia, Ghana, Belgium, the UK and Sweden
As part of China Capital, reporters also examined hundreds of credit application forms and other records that partly explained why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal. The documents revealed the geopolitical nature of some loans.
In Australia, ICBC issued “loss-making or marginal loans” to some of the country’s biggest resources and infrastructure companies, including Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Glencore, as a way of starting long-term relationships that would help advance Beijing’s political goals, the Australian Financial Review found.
The documents show how in 2015, Andrew Forrest, the billionaire CEO of Fortescue, an iron ore miner, made an emergency trip to Beijing to meet with ICBC’s chairman and seek assistance after the company was forced to cancel a $2.5 billion bond issuance because of unattractive interest rates.
Fortescue was struggling financially, but ICBC’s Sydney branch implored the Beijing headquarters to approve the loan at rates close to 30% below those offered by bond investors in the U.S., AFR reported. An internal memo cited Fortescue’s “significant strategic importance for the Chinese steel industry.”
ICIJ media partners in Ghana found evidence of loans awarded for similarly strategic reasons.
Ghana Business News reported how ICBC continued to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to the Ghana Cocoa Board, a government entity that supports and controls the production of cocoa — an important commodity — even though the company lacked transparency and was on a watchlist of borrowers in financial distress.
According to internal records, China stood to benefit from financing the firm, also known as Cocobod, since Chinese trade companies were key buyers and the deal helped cement the political alliance between Beijing and Accra. ICBC’s Brussels branch also participated in the loan to Cocobod, De Tijd reported, suggesting that the overseas units often helped each other when the clients were considered strategic for the bank and the party-state.
ICBC acquired a key role in the China-Africa trade thanks to its 19.7% stake in South African banking giant Standard Bank, The Africa Report found. articles.title_orig: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.title_zh: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.content_orig:
America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
Long-standing educational programs such as Fulbright, Boren, and the Critical Language Scholarship are all suspended. A leader-level deal could bring them back and protect the students who take part.
- Rosie LevineExecutive Director of the U.S.-China Education Trust
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
Derk Bodde set out for Beijing in 1948 expecting to spend a quiet year translating an esoteric work of Chinese philosophy. Instead, as the first recipient of the newly created Fulbright fellowship in China, he found himself an eyewitness to the Chinese Communist Party’s takeover, and his account of what he saw became a rare firsthand record for policymakers, academics, and the American public. When China closed to foreign contact for the next quarter-century, Bodde’s expertise didn’t just remain useful: it was irreplaceable.
Bodde’s story is a clear example of the ways in which in-country research is a proven and often indispensable tool to strengthen American expertise of foreign countries—and not only with friendly nations. But as Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet tomorrow in Washington, DC, only around two thousand Americans are studying in China, down from fifteen thousand a decade ago, and the public and private ecosystem that once supported deep American study of China is collapsing precisely when it is needed most.
That decline is due both to funding cuts and legitimate concerns that students may face risks of arbitrary detention in China. Currently, two American academics have been designated as wrongfully detained after traveling to China for academic purposes, creating risks that must be addressed by Beijing. Such cases are rare—the vast majority of Americans who study in China do so without incident—but they are real, and their chilling effect reaches far beyond the individuals involved. At the upcoming summit, Presidents Trump and President Xi should elevate specific programs like Fulbright into leader-level deliverables, with President Xi’s high-profile support for them at the summit providing implicit assurances that participants will not face undue risks from China’s security services.
This approach has some precedent. Exchange programs sometimes receive broad protections from leaders. Indeed, even at the height of the Cold War, the United States established the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX) in 1968 as a formalized, bilateral academic exchange mechanism, sending generations of American Sovietologists into the Soviet Union, even as the two countries remained locked in rivalry. IREX and its successors, including the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People’s Republic of China, which managed similar style exchanges with China before diplomatic normalization, were established to lend U.S. government protection to academic exchanges deemed essential to the national interest.
By contrast, the China programs that built a generation of expertise are now defunct. The Fulbright Program has been suspended in China since 2020, partly over risks that participating students and researchers might be detained by China. Alongside Fulbright, less well-known but essential U.S. government–funded programs specifically designed to encourage greater foreign area expertise in government have been suspended to mainland China, including the Boren Awards, the Critical Language Scholarship, the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), and more.
At home, the area studies infrastructure in U.S. universities that was built in the 1950s, including the National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships, has been gutted amid cuts at the Department of Education. In recent weeks, new unclear federal restrictions on higher education’s ties to China have pushed some universities to conclude that even nonsensitive academic engagement—undergraduate study abroad included—carries too much risk: the University of North Carolina is the latest institution to pull down its study abroad program.
Critics of travel to China argue that Taiwan offers a safer alternative for Mandarin language study, and that the extent of state surveillance makes the risk of visiting China not worth the potential benefits. But Taiwan’s educational opportunities, while excellent, cannot fully substitute for the loss of access to China’s economy, society, and culture.
America needs a much deeper supply of China experts to handle a fast-changing relationship. In closed-door meetings compiled for the U.S.-China Education Trust’s 2026 report, America’s China Talent Challenge, stakeholders across the U.S. government, business, and academia described how their sectors depend on American expertise to interpret China’s actions—from geopolitics and security, to trade and supply chains—and to keep the United States competitive. The working group concluded that China expertise must be considered a national resource.
As Trump and Xi meet in Washington, progress on people-to-people diplomacy may be less challenging than in other domains. But both sides can take steps to improve the situation.
First, the Trump administration should negotiate with Beijing to elevate specific programs, from named legacy programs—including the Fulbright, Boren, Critical Language Scholarship, and NSLI-Y—to new initiatives, into summit deliverables. President Xi’s endorsement of these programs would provide implicit protection for those students who participate in them. President Trump could privately push to formalize assurances that participants will face no risks from China’s security services. And to make that gesture credible, Beijing should release detained academics.
Second, in tandem with these negotiations, the United States should reverse cuts to funding programs, which are in many cases entirely unrelated to China. The area studies infrastructure built nearly eighty years ago, to include National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and FLAS fellowships, has been gutted and should be restored. Congress should also fund new programs, purpose-built for today’s U.S.-China relationship. Scrutiny of university ties to China is in some cases warranted, but it should be scoped so that nonsensitive academic engagement, such as undergraduate study abroad and language programs, are able to proceed with appropriate safeguards.
To some, these proposals may seem unrealistic. But they are rooted in history and pragmatism. Washington has long had educational programs in countries with competitors and adversaries. Those programs were often sustained by leader-level understandings that they would be insulated from competitive dynamics in the relationship. Improving mutual understanding is inherently valuable. For both Washington and Beijing, it also reduces the risk of miscalculation. If the next generation of policymakers has no China experience, both countries will suffer.
A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, or track policy implementation on the ground is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable. Rebuilding China expertise is not an act of goodwill toward Beijing. It is a hard-nosed investment in the United States’ atrophying ability to understand and compete with its most consequential rival.
The United States and China have few bright spots in the bilateral relationship, and fewer still that could be elevated into summit deliverables. Naming and insulating a handful of exchange programs from political and security pressures is in fact one of the most straightforward areas for cooperation that exists between the two countries.

articles.content_orig:
The U.S. is open to discussing shared risks with China in upcoming AI talks this weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration has flatly rejected calls from industry to pace or slow down the development of AI, citing a fierce race against China.
Bessent's scheduled meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng could provide an opening for talks on U.S.-China AI safety cooperation.
"The United States remains the leader in AI. And we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems. We expect our discussions to cover both open and closed weight models," Bessent said in a statement to Axios.
"Bessent and [United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer] are the point guys on China. So it makes sense the secretary is in this position," a senior administration official said.
Driving the news: There will be multi-hour meetings in New York City, focused on AI, trade, rare earths, and other economic issues, building on previous discussions held in cities around the world, sources familiar said.
The agenda will remain flexible to allow for substantive discussion across the range of relevant issues, sources added.
Possible working-level meetings will continue into Monday, sources said.
Catch up quick: Bessent has played a key role in the Trump administration's AI agenda.
He was among the few cabinet members who flanked President Trump during a G7 press conference in June, where top AI CEOs and the administration discussed a U.S.-led effort to coordinate global AI standards.
Bessent also helped cool Anthropic's relations with the administration following a fallout with the Pentagon and is viewed as a reasonable actor who is trusted by the private sector and critical infrastructure operators, sources familiar have previously told Axios.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick led high-profile AI discussions during the G20 summit in North Carolina earlier this month, while Bessent is taking the lead on talks with China.
The big picture: Bessent's meetings in New York come days before Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's summit in Washington on Sept. 24.
AI CEOs have been calling for U.S.-China coordination on safety standards.
"All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said this week, while pushing back on U.S. AI companies' calls to slow down and warning against "fear-mongering."
The bottom line: While a major breakthrough in U.S.-China safety cooperation remains a tall order, Bessent's involvement signals room for engagement on AI between the competing countries.
